answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Gandhi’s response was published in his weekly journal ‘Young India’ on 2 April 1931, drawn from his press remarks after the execution of the revolutionary Bhagat Singh. The wording is confirmed by his ‘Collected Works’ and by quotation references citing that date.

source.excerpt: What is true of individuals is true of nations. One cannot forgive too much. The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.
trail: The line closes a statement Gandhi published in ‘Young India’ on 2 April 1931; quotation archives such as LibQuotes cite that exact date.
He wrote it after failing to win clemency for the revolutionary Bhagat Singh, hanged on 23 March 1931 — the episode is documented at mkgandhi.org.
It is often re-sourced to the 1958 UNESCO anthology ‘All Men Are Brothers’, which reprints Gandhi’s words but is not their origin.
Gandhi’s complete writings are preserved in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version keeps only the last two sentences
source.excerptNote: The famous two sentences are the close of a longer reflection Gandhi gave the press after Bhagat Singh’s hanging — he was answering whether it was naive for a nation to forgive the empire that ruled it.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: Mahatma Gandhi
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, called Mahatma (‘great-souled’), led India’s nonviolent movement for independence and became the global exponent of satyagraha — truth-force, or nonviolent resistance. A London-trained lawyer who first honed his methods fighting discrimination in South Africa, he placed forgiveness and self-suffering at the centre of his political ethics. He was assassinated in January 1948.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Gandhi wrote these words in the rawest political moment of 1931. He had just signed the Gandhi–Irwin Pact with the British and had pressed — unsuccessfully — for the death sentences on Bhagat Singh and his comrades to be commuted. When the three were hanged on 23 March, many Indians blamed Gandhi for not making their reprieve a condition of the pact. Pressed by the press on whether forgiving such a government was mere weakness, he answered that the opposite was true.

‘What is true of individuals is true of nations,’ he said. ‘One cannot forgive too much. The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.’ For Gandhi, forgiveness was not surrender but the hardest exercise of strength — a claim that recast nonviolence as power rather than passivity.
detailsBody: The line is frequently reprinted from ‘All Men Are Brothers’, the UNESCO-sponsored 1958 anthology of Gandhi’s writings, and quote sites such as Goodreads name that book as the source. The anthology only reproduces the passage; its origin is the 1931 ‘Young India’ statement, decades earlier.

Stripped of its setting, the quote now circulates as a stand-alone maxim about personal forgiveness. In its original context it was a comment on how a newly assertive nation should regard the empire that had just executed its revolutionaries.
